packages.title: Air-pollutant versus greenhouse-gas separation QA
facts: Defra air-pollutant statistics cover pollutants including NOx, ammonia, sulphur dioxide and particulate matter.
Air pollutants and greenhouse gases overlap in some source activities but are not interchangeable pollutant sets.
A reduction in an air pollutant does not imply the same percentage reduction in CO2e.
Air-pollutant inventories use pollutant-specific emission factors and reporting conventions.
No parcel greenhouse-gas value is inferred from air-pollutant totals.

packages.title: Air-pollutant 2024 inventory-vintage QA
facts: The 2026 UK air-pollutant inventory materials include historical emissions through 2024.
The air-pollutant statistical release was updated on 12 February 2026.
Reference year 2024 must be preserved when comparing with later monitoring or policy data.
Inventory-year emissions are estimates rather than real-time air-quality readings.
No 2026 parcel emission is inferred from a 2024 inventory value.

packages.title: NAEI historical versus projected emissions QA
facts: NAEI publishes historical air-quality emissions data for 1990 to 2024 in the 2026 inventory cycle.
NAEI separately publishes projected air-quality emissions for 2025 to 2050.
Historical inventory values and projections are different statistical products.
Projected values must not be labelled observed emissions.
Neither product directly provides parcel greenhouse-gas emissions.

packages.title: NAEI gridded and point-source vintage QA
facts: NAEI lists gridded emissions and large point-source datasets separately from national historical tables.
The listed gridded and point-source products use specific reference-year vintages rather than live data.
Grid cells and point sources are different spatial representations.
A grid value is not automatically a cadastral parcel value and a point source may span multiple parcels.
Spatial joins require explicit geometry and source-year checks.

packages.title: England residual-waste 2024 total and per-capita QA
facts: Defra estimates 58.4 million tonnes of residual waste in England in 2024.
The estimate is 0.5% lower than the 58.7 million tonnes reported for 2023.
The 2024 estimate corresponds to 996 kilograms per person.
Waste mass and per-capita waste are activity metrics rather than greenhouse-gas totals.
No parcel emissions are calculated from the national waste estimate.

packages.title: Residual-waste landfill 37.8 Mt QA
facts: Defra estimates residual waste sent to landfill fell to 37.8 million tonnes in 2024.
The comparable 2019 estimate was 45.5 million tonnes.
The reported 2019-to-2024 decrease is 16.8% by mass.
Landfill tonnage is not the same measure as landfill methane or CO2e emissions.
A waste-emissions factor is not silently applied to derive parcel GHG.

packages.title: Residual-waste incineration 18.9 Mt QA
facts: Defra estimates 18.9 million tonnes of residual waste went through incineration including Energy from Waste in 2024.
The comparable 2019 estimate was 16.1 million tonnes.
The reported increase over the period is 16.9% by mass.
Incinerated waste mass is not identical to combustion greenhouse-gas emissions or displaced-energy savings.
No site or parcel carbon value is inferred from the mass statistic.

packages.title: Waste-management activity versus GHG QA
facts: Defra waste statistics combine administrative sources and surveys across waste-generation and management topics.
Waste-management quantities can be reported as tonnes, treatment routes or recycling outcomes.
Those quantities are not greenhouse-gas measurements unless a specific carbon method is applied.
Different waste streams and treatment routes have different emissions profiles.
No generic tonnes-to-CO2e conversion is applied at parcel level.

packages.title: England drought restrictions population-share QA
facts: The Environment Agency reported that almost 40% of England's population faced water-use restrictions in the 17 to 23 July 2026 summary.
The restrictions included temporary-use bans by multiple water companies.
The statistic describes water-demand and resilience conditions rather than greenhouse-gas emissions.
Population under restrictions is not a measure of water abstraction volume.
No parcel emissions value is inferred from restriction coverage.

packages.title: Drought abstraction-licence restrictions QA
facts: The Environment Agency reported 1,353 abstraction-licence restrictions during the cited July 2026 drought period.
The restrictions reflect low-flow and water-resource conditions.
A count of restricted licences does not state the volume of water abstracted.
Water-resource restrictions are not greenhouse-gas emissions observations.
No restricted licence is mapped to a parcel without an explicit licence and geometry join.

packages.title: Drought water-demand versus GHG QA
facts: The July 2026 drought summary links several temporary-use bans predominantly to high demand or resilience concerns.
The Environment Agency also reports agricultural impacts, low river flows and environmental incidents.
High water demand is an operational pressure rather than a direct carbon-emissions measure.
Drought conditions can affect energy and agriculture but do not provide a universal emissions factor.
No causal parcel GHG estimate is inferred from drought status.

packages.title: Water-abstraction 20 cubic-metre licensing-threshold QA
facts: Environment Agency guidance states abstractions above 20 cubic metres per day are likely to require an abstraction licence.
The 20 cubic metre figure is a regulatory threshold, not an observed abstraction volume for a site.
The guidance covers surface-water and groundwater sources including rivers, reservoirs, springs and aquifers.
Licence status does not state the energy used to pump or treat the water.
No greenhouse-gas value is inferred from the licensing threshold.

packages.title: Weekly EPC 23 July 2026 statistics-in-development QA
facts: ONS published the 23 July 2026 edition of the weekly Energy Performance Building Certificates dataset.
The dataset reports weekly numbers of EPCs for new and existing domestic properties in England and Wales.
ONS labels these weekly indicators as official statistics in development.
An EPC count is a certificate-lodgement activity measure rather than a measured energy-consumption series.
No parcel emissions value is inferred from weekly certificate counts.
